citation: Griffiths, W. E., Hill, R. C. and Judge, G. G. (1993), Learning and Practicing Econometrics, Wiley, Table 15.4 -- the 38-household food-expenditure survey. The same 38 rows are the application of Ferrari, S. L. P. and Cribari-Neto, F. (2004), Beta Regression for Modelling Rates and Proportions, Journal of Applied Statistics 31(7), 799-815, DOI 10.1080/0266476042000214501, section 4, and are distributed verbatim as statsmodels/othermod/tests/results/foodexpenditure.csv in statsmodels 0.14.6.
notes:
THE TWO COVARIATES OF THE PUBLISHED REGRESSION, transcribed from the source as printed: `income` is household income and `persons` is the number of people living in the household. Both are written as floats although `persons` is a count, because a design matrix is one numeric block and the beta regression treats it as a measurement -- the published model enters it linearly and estimates one coefficient for it.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SUPPORT. The response is not here: it is the share of income spent on food, and the companion dataset ferrari_cribari_neto_2004_food_share carries it. `income` therefore appears in this study twice, as the divisor of the response and as a covariate, which is the specification the paper fits and not an accident of this transcription. There is no intercept column: the wrapper adds its own and refuses a design that brings one. The two datasets share this index and a case that reaches for one must reach for the other.
